I lived in Scotland while growing up and the traffic wardens (the dudes that give out parking fines for illegally parked cars or expired parking meters) were paid by the region (the Scottish equivalent of the state) or the city from taxpayer money. At one point in my home town they privatized the service and it had a marked effect on the number of tickets written and the public's attitude toward the wardens... To the point where the wardens started traveling in pairs and carrying pepper spray for protection.

There were rumors that the new wardens were paid on commission, and this was offered as an explanation as to why they were so quick to ticket, but I think the reality was that they were now under pressure from their employers to generate revenue and so were excessively aggressive in their ticketing practices and this lead to widespread disapproval and, being Scotland, it got a bit violent at times. It got to the point where the traffic wardens were wearing stab proof vests and other tactical clothing, looking very much like unarmed mercenaries.

So when I moved to the US and I saw how the police here fund themselves I couldn't but help draw the same conclusions you have. It seems like an obvious problem to avoid, that it's bound to breed some sort of division between the PD and the public. It's a minor issue when you look at it as just excessive parking/speeding tickets and so on, but then add in the social and cultural issues the US deals with, racial divides, poverty lines, aggressive political rivalries, all that shit, then you have the perfect fertilizer for a society that hates it's own police force.

What (educated) pro's and con's do you see on Voat incorporating in the US?

I've lived in the US for 16 years before moving back to Western Europe, and I've worked with startups getting established there. So I hope I can give some insights:

Pros:

  1. Easier access to capital. I believe this is the main reason why Voat got incorporated there. Generally, angel investors and venture capitalists who would invest into Voat at this stage, don't want to keep a company indefinitely. They invest into a portfolio of companies, with the expectation that they'd cash out in about 10 years of time. Within that time frame, some companies will fail, while others succeed, and the hope is that the net return will be positive. The exit strategy from an investment at this stage usually has one of two methods: sale to a larger company or float on the stock exchange. Both are easier to achieve when the company is governed by US corporate laws, given that most potential buyers are there.
  2. Freedom of speech. This is a nice marketing gimmick for Voat's members, but also somewhat true. Freedom of speech in the US is far more open: There are no federal laws against inciting violence against minorities (Sweden), promotion of unpopular political movements (Germany), libel laws (UK) or laws actions against portals not moderating user comments (EU. In this regard, posting whatever you want may be easier in the US than elsewhere. However...

Cons

  1. Freedom after speech. This is the main problem with incorporating in the US. As numerous cases show, freedom after speech is not guaranteed, and you can get hassled by everybody from the lowest district attorney to the FBI. Your opinions may strike a raw nerve of some uptight bureaucrat with sand in her vagina, a corporation, or simply say something that may be considered as whistleblowing.
  2. Privacy. The US is notorious for forcing Web portals to disclose the identities or private communication of its members. In the case of Voat, this can mean the IP address of the individual or private messages (remember, not everything on this site is public). Moreover, Voat could get slapped with a gag order, not allowing the site to notify anyone that they were forced to disclose any private information. (Fortunately, this can be somewhat prevented by having a warrant canary.)

All in all, incorporating anywhere would be a tradeoff. The US is currently the least of all evils, but I'd like to see smaller nations (Iceland, tax haven countries) to become free data brokers who'd guarantee both: freedom of speech and freedom after speech. I'm sure their digital economy would greatly profit from it.

This is the kind of response this thread needed. Not knocking most of the other responses, it's just helpful to get the point of view of someone who has experienced living in the US, and other places as well.
